questions.stem: Which structure is classified as an organelle in this syllabus?

options.text: The cytoplasm surrounding the cell components
options.why: Cytoplasm is excluded from the syllabus definition of an organelle. It’s the cell material in which many organelles are located.

options.text: The cellulose cell wall outside the membrane
options.why: The cell wall is a cell structure, but the syllabus doesn’t classify it as an organelle.

options.text: A ribosome translating an mRNA molecule
options.why: A ribosome is a discrete subunit adapted for protein synthesis. An organelle doesn’t have to be surrounded by a membrane.

options.text: The cytoskeleton extending throughout the cytoplasm
options.why: The cytoskeleton has important cellular functions, but it’s excluded from the organelle category used here.

questions.stem: What did cell fractionation combined with ultracentrifugation allow researchers to do?

options.text: Separate cell components into fractions and test their biochemical activities
options.why: Separating components produces fractions enriched in particular organelles. Researchers can then test what reactions occur in each fraction.

options.text: Observe living organelles at the resolution of an electron microscope
options.why: Electron microscopy can reveal fine structure, but it doesn’t keep specimens alive. Fractionation is used to isolate components.

options.text: Separate organelles according to the colors they absorb under visible light
options.why: Centrifugation separates components using physical properties such as size and density, not their visible color.

options.text: Identify every organelle without breaking the plasma membrane of the cell
options.why: Cell fractionation begins by breaking cells open. It can’t isolate internal structures while every plasma membrane remains intact.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of separating the nucleus from the cytoplasm?

options.text: Translation can occur before an RNA transcript has been completed
options.why: That can occur in prokaryotes because there’s no nuclear envelope. Eukaryotic compartmentalization prevents this immediate contact.

options.text: mRNA can be modified before it encounters cytoplasmic ribosomes
options.why: Transcription and RNA processing occur in the nucleus, while translation occurs outside it. The envelope keeps those stages separate.

options.text: Ribosomes can enter the nucleus and translate genes beside the DNA
options.why: Translation occurs outside the nucleus. Ribosomal components pass through pores, but active cytoplasmic translation doesn’t move beside the DNA.

options.text: DNA can leave through nuclear pores and attach directly to rough ER
options.why: DNA is retained in the nucleus. Processed mRNA carries the genetic message through nuclear pores to ribosomes.

questions.stem: Why can concentrating enzymes and metabolites in a compartment increase reaction rate?

options.text: The compartment permanently lowers the activation energy without an enzyme
options.why: Enzymes lower activation energy. A compartment supports their action by bringing enzymes and substrates together.

options.text: The membrane converts every reaction in the compartment into active transport
options.why: Active transport moves substances across membranes. It doesn’t describe the metabolic reactions occurring inside a compartment.

options.text: The concentrated reactants undergo more frequent enzyme-substrate collisions
options.why: Keeping enzymes and substrates in a smaller region raises their local concentrations, so productive collisions can occur more frequently.

options.text: The enclosed metabolites stop moving and remain attached to enzymes
options.why: Molecules still move within a compartment. Their concentration, rather than a loss of movement, raises the collision frequency.

questions.stem: A lysosome fuses with a phagocytic vacuole. What advantage does this provide?

options.text: Hydrolytic enzymes digest engulfed material inside an isolated compartment
options.why: Fusion places enzymes and engulfed material together while a membrane separates digestion from the rest of the cytoplasm.

options.text: Ribosomes translate the engulfed material into proteins for the cell
options.why: Ribosomes translate mRNA, not engulfed particles. The vacuole-lysosome system digests the material with hydrolytic enzymes.

options.text: The vacuole exposes the entire cytoplasm to hydrolytic enzymes
options.why: That would risk damage to the cell. Compartmentalization keeps the digestive reactions separated from the cytosol.

options.text: The lysosome converts the vacuole into a site of transcription
options.why: Transcription uses DNA in the nucleus. Lysosomes and phagocytic vacuoles are involved in intracellular digestion.

questions.stem: How does the small volume of a mitochondrion's intermembrane space support ATP production?

options.text: It allows a given number of pumped protons to produce a steep concentration gradient
options.why: A small volume undergoes a large concentration change when protons enter it. This helps establish the gradient used by ATP synthase.

options.text: It provides extra room for all enzymes of the Krebs cycle to spread apart
options.why: Krebs cycle enzymes and substrates are compartmentalized in the matrix, not the intermembrane space.

options.text: It prevents protons from passing through ATP synthase in the inner membrane
options.why: Proton movement through ATP synthase drives ATP production. Preventing that movement would stop chemiosmosis.

options.text: It stores glucose before glycolysis begins inside the mitochondrion
options.why: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol. The intermembrane space is important for proton accumulation, not glucose storage.

questions.stem: What is the benefit of cristae in a mitochondrion?

options.text: They enlarge the matrix so more glycolysis can occur
options.why: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol, and cristae are inner-membrane folds rather than extensions of the matrix.

options.text: They increase inner-membrane area for electron transport chains and ATP synthase
options.why: Cristae provide more inner membrane on which oxidative phosphorylation can occur.

options.text: They separate nuclear transcription from cytoplasmic translation
options.why: That separation is produced by the nuclear envelope. Cristae belong to mitochondria.

options.text: They contain the enzymes and substrates of the Calvin cycle
options.why: The Calvin cycle occurs in the chloroplast stroma. Cristae support aerobic respiration in mitochondria.

questions.stem: Which chloroplast feature directly provides a large area for the light-dependent reactions?

options.text: The double membrane around the chloroplast envelope
options.why: The envelope separates the chloroplast from the cytoplasm. The light-dependent machinery is located on thylakoid membranes.

options.text: The enzyme-containing fluid of the chloroplast stroma
options.why: The stroma contains Calvin cycle enzymes. It isn’t the membrane bearing photosystems and electron carriers.

options.text: The extensive system of internal thylakoid membranes
options.why: Thylakoid membranes contain photosystems, electron carriers and ATP synthase, so their large area supports the light-dependent reactions.

options.text: The narrow space between the two envelope membranes
options.why: This space isn’t the thylakoid lumen. Proton accumulation for photosynthesis occurs inside thylakoids.

questions.stem: Where are the enzymes and substrates of the Calvin cycle compartmentalized?

options.text: In the mitochondrial matrix
options.why: The mitochondrial matrix contains Krebs cycle enzymes and substrates. It belongs to aerobic respiration.

options.text: In the thylakoid lumen
options.why: The thylakoid lumen is the small compartment where protons accumulate during the light-dependent reactions.

options.text: In the chloroplast stroma
options.why: The stroma is the enzyme-containing fluid surrounding the thylakoids, and it’s where the Calvin cycle occurs.

options.text: In the nuclear envelope
options.why: The nuclear envelope separates the nucleus from the cytoplasm. It has no role as the site of the Calvin cycle.

questions.stem: Why does the nuclear envelope break down during mitosis and meiosis?

options.text: To release DNA for translation by cytoplasmic ribosomes
options.why: Ribosomes translate mRNA, not DNA. Envelope breakdown allows chromosome movement rather than DNA translation.

options.text: To let lysosomes digest chromosomes before daughter cells form
options.why: Chromosomes must be preserved and separated. Lysosomal digestion would destroy genetic material.

options.text: To allow spindle microtubules to interact with and move chromosomes
options.why: Removing the nuclear boundary gives the spindle access to the chromosomes during nuclear division.

options.text: To attach rough ER ribosomes directly to the chromosomes
options.why: Rough ER ribosomes synthesize proteins from mRNA. They don’t need direct contact with chromosomes.

questions.stem: Which protein is most likely to be synthesized by a ribosome bound to rough ER?

options.text: A cytosolic enzyme retained where it is synthesized
options.why: A protein retained in the cytosol is usually synthesized on a free ribosome.

options.text: A protein that will be secreted from the cell
options.why: Proteins for secretion enter the rough ER during synthesis and then travel through the endomembrane system.

options.text: A histone that will remain associated with nuclear DNA
options.why: Histones are made on free ribosomes and then imported into the nucleus.

options.text: An enzyme that will carry out glycolysis in the cytosol
options.why: Cytosolic enzymes are retained inside the cell and are generally synthesized by free ribosomes.

questions.stem: What is the main role of the Golgi apparatus in protein secretion?

options.text: It transcribes genes into mRNA and sends the transcripts to ribosomes
options.why: Transcription occurs in the nucleus. The Golgi acts on proteins that have already been synthesized.

options.text: It produces ATP to power translation on the rough ER
options.why: Mitochondria produce most ATP by aerobic respiration. The Golgi processes and packages proteins.

options.text: It processes, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles
options.why: Proteins arrive from the rough ER, pass through Golgi cisternae and leave in vesicles for their destinations.

options.text: It digests engulfed microorganisms using hydrolytic enzymes
options.why: That describes lysosomes acting with phagocytic vacuoles. It isn’t the Golgi’s role in secretion.

questions.stem: What role does clathrin play in vesicle transport?

options.text: It coats a membrane region and helps curve it into a budding vesicle
options.why: Clathrin assembles as a coat that helps shape a membrane bud. The coat is removed before the vesicle completes later transport steps.

options.text: It remains inside every vesicle as the substance being transported
options.why: Clathrin is a temporary coat protein on the cytosolic surface, not the cargo enclosed by every vesicle.

options.text: It forms nuclear pores that select which mRNA leaves the nucleus
options.why: Nuclear pore complexes control transport through the nuclear envelope. Clathrin helps form coated vesicles.

options.text: It catalyzes protein synthesis while attached to rough ER membranes
options.why: Ribosomes catalyze protein synthesis. Clathrin acts during the formation of particular vesicles.
